Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

This is a list of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_(planet) "Mercury (planet)"), the [innermost planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_planets "Inner planets") of the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") *(for other features, see [list of geological features on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_geological_features_on_Mercury "List of geological features on Mercury"))*.[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) Most Mercurian craters [are named after](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") famous writers, artists and composers. According to the rules by IAU's [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"), all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.[[6]](#cite_note-Ritzel-7) Craters larger than 250 km in diameter are referred to as "basins" *(also see [§ Terminology](#Terminology))*.[[7]](#cite_note-8)[[8]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-9)

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_craters_on_Mercury&action=edit), there are 444 named Mercurian craters,[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2) a small fraction of the total number of named Solar System craters, most of which are [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"), [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") and [Venerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Venus "List of craters on Venus") craters.[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-5)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-6)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

Mercury

The planet Mercury has just under 400 craters. The wonderful part is that most of them are named for famous people in the arts: writers, artists and composers. The rule for inclusion is that “all new craters must be named after an artist that was famous for more than fifty years, and dead for more than three years, before the date they are named.”

*Haydn: Symphony No. 43 in E-Flat Major, Hob.I:43, “Mercury” – IV. Allegro (Orchestra of the Age of Enlightenment; Frans Brüggen, cond.)*

In looking over the list, we find some 50 craters named after composers, conductors, and musicians. [Gluck](https://interlude.hk/skipping-town-christoph-willibald-gluck/) and [Debussy](https://interlude.hk/claude-achille-debussy/) rub shoulders with John Lennon and Machaut. They come from countries all over the world, from India to Italy, Austria to America, and China to Brazil. They are predominantly male, but [Alicia de Larrocha](https://interlude.hk/great-women-artists-shaped-music-v-alicia-de-larrocha/) (Spain) does sweep in as does Cai Wenji (China) and Umm Kulthum (Egypt).

*Strauss I: Merkurs Flugel, Walzer (Wings of Mercury, Waltz), Op. 83 (Slovak Sinfonietta, Žilina; Christian Pollack, cond.)*

**Aaron Copland** ([/ˈkoʊplənd/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*KOHP-lənd*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) November 14, 1900 – December 2, 1990) was an American composer, critic, writer, teacher, pianist, and conductor of his own and other American music. Copland was referred to by his peers and critics as the "Dean of American Music". The open, slowly changing harmonies in much of his music are typical of what many consider the sound of American music, evoking the vast American landscape and pioneer spirit. He is best known for the works he wrote in the 1930s and 1940s in a deliberately accessible style often referred to as "populist" and which he called his "vernacular" style.[[3]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack1999186-3) Works in this vein include the ballets *[Appalachian Spring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appalachian_Spring "Appalachian Spring")*, *[Billy the Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_the_Kid_(ballet) "Billy the Kid (ballet)")* and *[Rodeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodeo_(ballet) "Rodeo (ballet)")*, his *[Fanfare for the Common Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanfare_for_the_Common_Man "Fanfare for the Common Man")* and [Third Symphony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._3_(Copland) "Symphony No. 3 (Copland)"). In addition to his ballets and orchestral works, he produced music in many other genres, including chamber music, vocal works, opera, and film scores.

After some initial studies with composer [Rubin Goldmark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubin_Goldmark "Rubin Goldmark"), Copland traveled to Paris, where he first studied with [Isidor Philipp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isidor_Philipp "Isidor Philipp") and [Paul Vidal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Vidal "Paul Vidal"), then with noted pedagogue [Nadia Boulanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nadia_Boulanger "Nadia Boulanger"). He studied three years with Boulanger, whose eclectic approach to music inspired his own broad taste. Determined upon his return to the U.S. to make his way as a full-time composer, Copland gave lecture-recitals, wrote works on commission and did some teaching and writing. But he found that composing orchestral music in a [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism_(music) "Modernism (music)") style, which he had adopted while studying abroad, was unprofitable, particularly in light of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"). He shifted in the mid-1930s to a more accessible musical style that mirrored the German idea of *[Gebrauchsmusik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gebrauchsmusik "Gebrauchsmusik")* ("music for use"), music that could serve utilitarian and artistic purposes. During the Depression years, he traveled extensively to Europe, Africa, and Mexico, formed an important friendship with Mexican composer [Carlos Chávez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Chávez "Carlos Chávez"), and began composing his signature works.

During the late 1940s, Copland became aware that [Stravinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stravinsky "Stravinsky") and other fellow composers had begun to study [Arnold Schoenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnold_Schoenberg "Arnold Schoenberg")'s use of [twelve-tone (serial) techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twelve-tone_technique "Twelve-tone technique"). After he had been exposed to the works of French composer [Pierre Boulez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Boulez "Pierre Boulez"), he incorporated serial techniques into his *Piano Quartet* (1950), *Piano Fantasy* (1957), *[Connotations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Connotations_(Copland) "Connotations (Copland)")* for orchestra (1961), and *[Inscape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inscape_(Copland) "Inscape (Copland)")* for orchestra (1967). Unlike Schoenberg, Copland used his tone rows in much the same fashion as his tonal material—as sources for melodies and harmonies, rather than as complete statements in their own right, except for crucial events from a structural point of view. From the 1960s onward, Copland's activities turned more from composing to conducting. He became a frequent guest conductor of orchestras in the U.S. and the UK and made a series of recordings of his music, primarily for [Columbia Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_Records "Columbia Records").

### Early years

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Aaron_Copland&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

Aaron Copland was born in [Brooklyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn "Brooklyn"), New York, on November 14, 1900.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199915-4) He was the youngest of five children in a [Conservative Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Jewish "Conservative Jewish") immigrant family of [Lithuanian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuanian_Jews "Lithuanian Jews") origin.[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198419-5) While emigrating from Russia to the United States, Copland's father, Harris Morris Copland, lived and worked in Scotland for two to three years to pay for his boat fare to the United States. It was there that Copland's father may have [Anglicized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglicized "Anglicized") his surname "Kaplan" to "Copland", though Copland himself believed for many years that the change had been caused by an [Ellis Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellis_Island "Ellis Island") immigration official when his father entered the country.[[4]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199915-4)[[6]](#cite_note-Cone-6) Copland was unaware until late in his life that the family name had been Kaplan, his parents having never told him.[[6]](#cite_note-Cone-6) Throughout his childhood, Copland and his family lived above his parents' Brooklyn shop, H. M. Copland's, at 628 Washington Avenue (which Aaron later called "a kind of neighborhood [Macy's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macy's "Macy's")"),[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199916-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) on the corner of Dean Street and Washington Avenue,[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoss2007266-9) and most of the children helped out in the store. His father was a staunch Democrat. The family members were active in [Congregation Baith Israel Anshei Emes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregation_Baith_Israel_Anshei_Emes "Congregation Baith Israel Anshei Emes"), where Aaron celebrated his [bar mitzvah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_mitzvah "Bar mitzvah"),[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199926-10) for which he studied under [Israel Goldfarb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Goldfarb "Israel Goldfarb").[[11]](#cite_note-jmrc-11) Not especially athletic, the sensitive young man became an avid reader and often read [Horatio Alger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Alger "Horatio Alger") stories on his front steps.[[12]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195315-12)

Copland's father had no musical interest. His mother, Sarah Mittenthal Copland, sang, played the piano, and arranged music lessons for her children.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199919-13) Copland had four older siblings: two brothers, Ralph and Leon, and two sisters, Laurine and Josephine.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) Of his siblings, his oldest brother Ralph was the most advanced musically; he was proficient on the violin. Laurine had the strongest connection with Aaron; she gave him his first piano lessons, promoted his musical education, and supported him in his musical career.[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199919-13) A student at the Metropolitan Opera School and frequent opera-goer, Laurine also brought home [libretti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libretti "Libretti") for Aaron to study.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195317-16) Copland attended [Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boys_High_School_(Brooklyn) "Boys High School (Brooklyn)") and in the summer went to various camps. Most of his early exposure to music was at Jewish weddings and ceremonies, and occasional family musicales.[[10]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199926-10)

Copland began writing songs at the age of eight and a half.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17) His earliest notated music, about seven bars he wrote when age 11, was for an opera scenario he created and called *Zenatello*.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17)[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199932-18) From 1913 to 1917 he took piano lessons with Leopold Wolfsohn, who taught him the standard classical fare.[[17]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198422-17) Copland's first public music performance was at a [Wanamaker's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wanamaker's "Wanamaker's") recital.[[19]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith195318-19)[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoplandPerlis198423-20) By age 15, after attending a concert by Polish composer-pianist [Ignacy Jan Paderewski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ignacy_Jan_Paderewski "Ignacy Jan Paderewski"), Copland decided to become a composer.[[21]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollack199933-21) At 16, he heard his first symphony, at the [Brooklyn Academy of Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Academy_of_Music "Brooklyn Academy of Music").[[22]](#cite_note-nyclgbtsites.org-22) After attempts to further his music study from a [correspondence course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correspondence_course "Correspondence course"), C

**Alicia de Larrocha y de la Calle** (23 May 1923 – 25 September 2009) was a Spanish [pianist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pianist "Pianist") and composer. She was considered one of the great piano legends of the 20th century.[[1]](#cite_note-1) [Reuters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters "Reuters") called her "the greatest Spanish pianist in history",[[2]](#cite_note-Renowned_Spanish_pianist_de_Larrocha_dead_at_86-2) *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* "one of the world's most outstanding pianists",[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3) and *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* "the leading Spanish pianist of her time".[[4]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha_obituary-4)

She won four [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"), out of fourteen nominations, and a [Prince of Asturias Award for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Asturias_Awards#Arts "Prince of Asturias Awards"). She is credited with bringing greater popularity to the compositions of [Isaac Albéniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Albéniz "Isaac Albéniz") and [Enrique Granados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Granados "Enrique Granados").[[2]](#cite_note-Renowned_Spanish_pianist_de_Larrocha_dead_at_86-2) In 1995, she became the first Spanish artist to win the [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") Prize.[[4]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha_obituary-4)

## Life and career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Alicia_de_Larrocha&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

Alicia de Larrocha was born in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), [Catalonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalonia "Catalonia"), Spain.[[5]](#cite_note-Pianist_Alicia_de_Larrocha_dies-5) She began studying piano with [Frank Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Marshall_(pianist) "Frank Marshall (pianist)") at the age of three, and later in life served as Director of his school, the Marshall Academy.[[6]](#cite_note-6) Both her parents were pianists and she was the niece of pianists.[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3)[[5]](#cite_note-Pianist_Alicia_de_Larrocha_dies-5) She gave her first public performance at the age of five at the [International Exposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1929_Barcelona_International_Exposition "1929 Barcelona International Exposition") in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona").[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3) She performed her first concert at the age of six at the [World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibero-American_Exposition_of_1929 "Ibero-American Exposition of 1929") in [Seville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seville "Seville") in 1929, and had her orchestral debut at the age of eleven. By 1943, her performances were selling out in Spain.[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3) She began touring internationally in 1947, and in 1954 toured North America with the [Los Angeles Philharmonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Philharmonic "Los Angeles Philharmonic"). In 1966, she engaged in a first tour of Southern Africa which proved so wildly popular that three further tours were completed[[7]](#cite_note-7) In 1969, de Larrocha performed in Boston for the [Peabody Mason Concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Mason_Concert "Peabody Mason Concert") series.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

De Larrocha, writes Jed Distler, "started composing at age seven and continued on and off until her 30th year, with a prolific spurt in her late teens," and while she never performed her works in public, she gave her family the choice of making them available after her death, which they have done.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

De Larrocha made numerous recordings of the solo piano repertoire and in particular the works of composers of her native Spain. She is best known for her recordings of the music of [Manuel de Falla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_de_Falla "Manuel de Falla"), [Enrique Granados](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Granados "Enrique Granados"), [Federico Mompou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federico_Mompou "Federico Mompou"), and [Isaac Albéniz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Albéniz "Isaac Albéniz"), as well as her 1967 recordings of [Antonio Soler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Soler_(composer) "Antonio Soler (composer)")'s keyboard sonatas. She recorded for [Hispavox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hispavox "Hispavox"), CBS/Columbia/Epic, BMG/RCA and London/Decca, winning her first [Grammy Award in 1975](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards_of_1975 "Grammy Awards of 1975") and her last one in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards_of_1992 "Grammy Awards of 1992"), at the age of almost seventy. She received the [Prince of Asturias Award for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_of_Asturias_Awards#Arts "Prince of Asturias Awards") in 1994.[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3)

De Larrocha spoke in a 1978 interview with Contemporary Keyboard,

> I don't believe there is a 'best' of anything in this life. I would say, though, that Granados was one of the great Spanish composers, and that, in my opinion, he was the only one that captured the real Romantic flavor. His style was aristocratic, elegant and poetic – completely different from Falla and Albéniz. To me, each of them is a different world. Falla was the one who really captured the spirit of the Gypsy music. And Albéniz, I think was more international than the others. Even though his music is Spanish in flavor, his style is completely Impressionistic.[[10]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-10)

Less than five feet tall and with small hands for a pianist,[[2]](#cite_note-Renowned_Spanish_pianist_de_Larrocha_dead_at_86-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3) spanning an interval of barely a tenth on the keyboard,[[11]](#cite_note-11) in her younger years she was nonetheless able to tackle all the big concertos ([all five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beethoven_piano_concertos "Beethoven piano concertos") by [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven"), [Liszt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Liszt "Franz Liszt")'s No. 1, [Brahms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Brahms "Johannes Brahms")'s [No. 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_Concerto_No._2_(Brahms) "Piano Concerto No. 2 (Brahms)"), [Rachmaninoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Rachmaninoff "Sergei Rachmaninoff")'s Nos. 2 and 3, both of [Ravel's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Ravel "Maurice Ravel"), and those of [Prokofiev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Prokofiev "Sergei Prokofiev"), [Bartók](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Béla_Bartók "Béla Bartók"), [Bliss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Bliss "Arthur Bliss") and [Khachaturian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aram_Khachaturian "Aram Khachaturian"), and many more), as well as the wide spans demanded by the music of Granados, Albéniz, and de Falla. She had a "long fifth finger" and a "wide stretch between thumb and index finger" which enhanced her technical ability.[[4]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha_obituary-4)

"She made her first recordings, of Chopin, at age nine, her feet not yet able to reach the pedals"[[12]](#cite_note-12) and was considered a great interpreter of Chopin.

As she grew older she began to play a different style of music; more [Mozart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Amadeus_Mozart "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart") and Beethoven were featured in her recitals and she became a regular guest at the "Mostly Mozart Festival" of the [Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincoln_Center_for_the_Performing_Arts "Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts") in New York. In 2001, she was named Honorary Member of the [Foundation for Iberian Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_for_Iberian_Music "Foundation for Iberian Music") at The City University of New York. De Larrocha retired from public performance in October 2003, aged 80, following a 76-year career.[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3)[[5]](#cite_note-Pianist_Alicia_de_Larrocha_dies-5)

She has performed with several major orchestras and conductors, including [Kurt Masur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Masur "Kurt Masur"), [Zubin Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zubin_Mehta "Zubin Mehta"), [Riccardo Muti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riccardo_Muti "Riccardo Muti"), [Charles Dutoit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dutoit "Charles Dutoit"), [Colin Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Davis "Colin Davis"), [Rafael Kubelik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rafael_Kubelík "Rafael Kubelík"), [André Previn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/André_Previn "André Previn"), [Georg Solti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Solti "Georg Solti"), [Seiji Ozawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seiji_Ozawa "Seiji Ozawa"), [Bernard Haitink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Haitink "Bernard Haitink"), [Wolfgang Sawallisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfgang_Sawallisch "Wolfgang Sawallisch"), [Eugen Jochum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_Jochum "Eugen Jochum"), [Claudio Abbado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Abbado "Claudio Abbado") and [Simon Rattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Rattle "Simon Rattle").

Alicia de Larrocha died on 25 September 2009 in Quiron Hospital, [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), aged 86. She had been in declining health since breaking her hip five years previously.[[10]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-10) Her husband, the pianist Juan Torra, with whom she had two children, had died in 1982.[[3]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha,_Renowned_Pianist,_Dies_at_86-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Alicia_de_Larrocha_obituary-4)

**Maya Angelou** ([/ˈændʒəloʊ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:En-us-Maya_Angelou.ogg "File:En-us-Maya Angelou.ogg") [*AN-jə-loh*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) born **Marguerite Annie Johnson**; April 4, 1928 – May 28, 2014) was an American [memoirist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoirist "Memoirist"), [essayist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essayist "Essayist"), [poet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet "Poet"), and [civil rights activist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_activist "Civil rights activist"). She published seven autobiographies, three books of essays, several books of poetry, and is credited with a list of plays, movies, and television shows spanning more than 50 years. She received dozens of awards and more than 50 honorary degrees.[[3]](#cite_note-whosehonor-3) Angelou's series of seven autobiographies focus on her childhood and early adult experiences. The first, *[I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Know_Why_the_Caged_Bird_Sings "I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings")* (1969), tells of her life up to the age of 17 and brought her international recognition and acclaim.

She became a poet and writer after a string of odd jobs during her young adulthood. In 1982, Angelou was named the first Reynolds Professor of American Studies at [Wake Forest University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wake_Forest_University "Wake Forest University") in [Winston-Salem, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston-Salem,_North_Carolina "Winston-Salem, North Carolina"). Angelou was active in the [Civil Rights Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Rights_Movement "Civil Rights Movement") and worked with [Martin Luther King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr. "Martin Luther King Jr.") and [Malcolm X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_X "Malcolm X"). Beginning in the 1990s, she made approximately 80 appearances a year on the [lecture circuit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lecture_circuit "Lecture circuit"), something she continued into her eighties. In 1993, Angelou recited her poem "[On the Pulse of Morning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Pulse_of_Morning "On the Pulse of Morning")" (1993) at the [first inauguration of Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Bill_Clinton "First inauguration of Bill Clinton"), making her the first poet to make an inaugural recitation since [Robert Frost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Frost "Robert Frost") at the [inauguration of John F. **Charles Edward Ives** ([/aɪvz/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); October 20, 1874 – May 19, 1954) was an American [modernist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernism_(music) "Modernism (music)") composer, actuary and businessman.[[1]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBotstein2001-1) Ives was among the earliest renowned American composers to achieve recognition on a global scale.[[2]](#cite_note-2) His music was largely ignored during his early career, and many of his works went unperformed for many years. Later in life, the quality of his music was publicly recognized through the efforts of contemporaries like [Henry Cowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cowell "Henry Cowell") and [Lou Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Harrison "Lou Harrison"), and he came to be regarded as an "American original".[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHall196442-5)

Ives was also among the first composers to engage in a systematic program of [experimental music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_music "Experimental music"), with [musical techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_technique "Musical technique") including [polytonality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytonality "Polytonality"), [polyrhythm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyrhythm "Polyrhythm"), [tone clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tone_cluster "Tone cluster"), [aleatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleatoric_music "Aleatoric music") elements, and [quarter tones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quarter_tone "Quarter tone").[[6]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBurkholder19954-6) The experimentation foreshadowed many musical innovations that were later more widely adopted during the 20th century; hence, Ives is often regarded as the leading American composer of art music of the 20th century.[[7]](#cite_note-Oxford_Grove_Online_-_Ives-7)

Sources of Ives's tonal imagery included [hymn tunes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn_tune "Hymn tune") and [traditional songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_songs "Traditional songs"); he also incorporated melodies of town bands at holiday parades, the fiddlers at Saturday night dances, patriotic songs, sentimental parlor ballads, and the melodies of [Stephen Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Foster "Stephen Foster").

## Early life and education

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Charles_Ives&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Ives was born in [Danbury, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danbury,_Connecticut "Danbury, Connecticut"), on October 20, 1874,[[8]](#cite_note-8) the son of George (Edward) Ives, a [US Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") bandleader in the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), and his wife, Mary Elizabeth Ives. The Iveses, descended from founding colonists of Connecticut, were one of Danbury's leading families, and they were prominent in business and civic improvement. They were similarly active in progressive social movements of the 19th century, including the abolition of slavery.[[7]](#cite_note-Oxford_Grove_Online_-_Ives-7)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

George Ives directed bands, choirs, and orchestras, and taught [music theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_theory "Music theory") and a number of instruments.[[10]](#cite_note-:0-10) Charles got his influences by sitting in the Danbury town square and listening to his father's marching band and other bands on other sides of the square [simultaneously](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simultaneity_(music) "Simultaneity (music)"). His father taught him and his brother (Joseph) Moss Ives (February 5, 1876 – April 7, 1939[[11]](#cite_note-11)) music,[[10]](#cite_note-:0-10) teaching [harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony "Harmony") and [counterpoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterpoint "Counterpoint") and guided his first compositions; George took an open-minded approach to theory, encouraging him to experiment in [bitonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitonal "Bitonal") and [polytonal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polytonality "Polytonality") harmonizations.[[7]](#cite_note-Oxford_Grove_Online_-_Ives-7) It was from him that Ives also learned the music of [Stephen Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Foster "Stephen Foster").[[12]](#cite_note-Grove-Ives-12) He became a church [organist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organist "Organist") at the age of 14[[13]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTECowellCowell195527-13) and wrote various hymns and songs for church services, including his *[Variations on "America"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variations_on_ "Variations on ")*, which he wrote for a [Fourth of July](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_of_July "Fourth of July") concert in [Brewster, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster,_New_York "Brewster, New York"). It is considered challenging even by modern concert organists, but he famously spoke of it as being "as much fun as playing [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball")", a commentary on his own organ technique at that age.[[14]](#cite_note-Grove,_Youth-14)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/38/Charles_Ives_pitcher.jpg/250px-Charles_Ives_pitcher.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Ives_pitcher.jpg)

Charles Ives, left, captain of the baseball team and pitcher for [Hopkins Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins_School "Hopkins School"), aged 18 (c. 1893)

Ives moved to [New Haven, Connecticut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Haven,_Connecticut "New Haven, Connecticut"), in 1893, enrolling in the [Hopkins School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopkins_School "Hopkins School"), where he captained the baseball team. In September 1894, Ives entered [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), studying under [Horatio Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horatio_Parker "Horatio Parker"). Here he composed in a choral style similar to his mentor, writing church music and even an 1896 campaign song for [William McKinley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_McKinley "William McKinley").[[15]](#cite_note-Grove,_Apprenticeship-15) On November 4, 1894, his father died, a crushing blow to him, but to a large degree, he continued the musical experimentation he had begun with him. His brother Moss later became a lawyer.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

At Yale, Ives was a prominent figure; he was a member of HeBoule, [Delta Kappa Epsilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Kappa_Epsilon "Delta Kappa Epsilon") (Phi chapter) and [Wolf's Head Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf's_Head_(secret_society) "Wolf's Head (secret society)"), and sat as chairman of the [Ivy Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy_League "Ivy League").[[15]](#cite_note-Grove,_Apprenticeship-15) He enjoyed sports at Yale and played on the varsity [American football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_football "American football") team. Michael C. Murphy, his coach, once remarked that it was a "crying shame" that he spent so much time at music as otherwise he could have been a champion sprinter.[[16]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoor1996[httpsbooksgooglecombooksid3zelh6aoP-sCpgPA411_411]-16) His works *[Calcium Light Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcium_Light_Night "Calcium Light Night")* and *Yale-Princeton Football Game* show the influence of college and sports on Ives's composition. He wrote his [Symphony No. 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._1_(Ives) "Symphony No. 1 (Ives)") as his senior thesis under Parker's supervision.[[15]](#cite_note-Grove,_Apprenticeship-15) Ives graduated from Yale in 1898, and continued his work as a church organist until May 1902.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

## Career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Charles_Ives&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Charles_Ives_grad_photo.jpg/250px-Charles_Ives_grad_photo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Charles_Ives_grad_photo.jpg)

Ives's graduation portrait from Yale University, c. June 1898

Following graduation, Ives started work in the [actuarial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actuary "Actuary") department of the [Mutual Life Insurance Company of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_Life_Insurance_Company_of_New_York "Mutual Life Insurance Company of New York").[[18]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGill2013[httpwwwcontingenciesonlinecomcontingenciesonline20130708pg27pg27_24]-18) In 1899, Ives moved to employment with the insurance agency Charles H. Raymond & Co., where he stayed until 1906. In 1907, upon the failure of Raymond & Co., he and his friend [Julian Myrick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Myrick "Julian Myrick") formed their own [insurance agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_agent "Insurance agent") Ives & Co., which later became Ives & Myrick, where he remained until he retired.[[19]](#cite_note-Grove,_Maturity-19)

During his career as an insurance executive and actuary, Ives devised creative ways to structure life-insurance packages for people of means, which laid the foundation of the modern practice of [estate planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estate_planning "Estate planning").[[20]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarolyi199610-20) His *Life Insurance with Relation to Inheritance Tax*, published in 1918, was well received. As a result of this he achieved considerable fame in the insurance industry of his time, with many of his business peers surprised to learn that he was also a composer. In his spare time, he composed music and, until his marriage, worked as an organist in Danbury and New Haven as well as [Bloomfield, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomfield,_New_Jersey "Bloomfield, New Jersey"), and New York City.[[15]](#cite_note-Grove,_Apprenticeship-15)

In 1907, Ives suffered the first of several "heart attacks" (as he and his family called them) that he had throughout his life. These attacks may have been psychological in origin rather than physical. Stuart Feder questions the legitimacy of these heart attacks, as he could not find any medical confirmation of them in previous reports. According to Feder, "For the only reliable information tells us that he suffered from palpitations, not pain, the cardinal symptom of heart attack."[[21]](#cite_note-21) Following his recovery from the 1907 attack, Ives entered into one of the most creative periods of his life as a composer.

Ives had a successful career in insurance. He also continued to be a prolific composer until he suffered another of several heart attacks in 1918, after which he composed very little. He wrote his last piece, the song "Sunrise", in August 1926.[[19]](#cite_note-Grove,_Maturity-19) In 1922, Ives published his *114 Songs*, which represents the breadth of his work as a composer—it includes [art songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_song "Art song"), songs he wrote as a teenager and young man, and highly [dissonant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonance_and_dissonance "Consonance and dissonance") songs such as "The Majority".[[19]](#cite_note-Grove,_Maturity-19)

According to his wife, one day in early 1927, Ives came downstairs with tears in his eyes. He could compose no more, he said; "nothing sounds right".[[22]](#cite_note-Grove,_Last_works-22) There have been numerous theories advanced to explain the silence of his late years. **Zenzile Miriam Makeba** ([/məˈkeɪbə/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [*mə-KAY-bə*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"),[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) Xhosa: [[máˈkʼêːɓà̤]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Nguni "Help:IPA/Nguni") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Zenzile_Miriam_Makeba_name.ogg "File:Zenzile Miriam Makeba name.ogg"); 4 March 1932 – 9 November 2008), nicknamed **Mama Africa**, was a South African singer, songwriter, actress, and [civil rights activist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_activist "Civil rights activist"). Associated with musical genres including [Afropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_popular_music "African popular music"), [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz"), and [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), she was an advocate against [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") and white-minority government in South Africa.

Born in [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg") to [Swazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swazi_people "Swazi people") and [Xhosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_people "Xhosa people") parents, Makeba was forced to find employment as a child after the death of her father. She had a brief and allegedly abusive first marriage at the age of 17, gave birth to her only child in 1950, and survived breast cancer. Her vocal talent had been recognized when she was a child, and she began singing professionally in the 1950s, with the Cuban Brothers, the [Manhattan Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan_Brothers "Manhattan Brothers"), and an all-woman group, [the Skylarks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Skylarks_(South_African_vocal_group) "The Skylarks (South African vocal group)"), performing a mixture of jazz, traditional African melodies, and Western popular music. In 1959, Makeba had a brief role in the anti-apartheid film *[Come Back, Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come_Back,_Africa "Come Back, Africa")*, which brought her international attention, and led to her performing in Venice, London, and New York City. In London, she met the American singer [Harry Belafonte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Belafonte "Harry Belafonte"), who became a mentor and colleague. She moved to New York City, where she became immediately popular, and recorded her first solo album in 1960. Her attempt to return to South Africa that year for her mother's funeral was prevented by the country's government.

Makeba's career flourished in the United States, and she released several albums and songs, her most popular being "[Pata Pata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pata_Pata "Pata Pata")" (1967). Along with Belafonte, she received a [Grammy Award for Best Folk Recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Ethnic_or_Traditional_Folk_Recording "Grammy Award for Best Ethnic or Traditional Folk Recording") for their 1965 album *[An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An_Evening_with_Belafonte/Makeba "An Evening with Belafonte/Makeba")*. She testified against the South African government at the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") and became involved in the [civil rights movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement "Civil rights movement"). She married [Stokely Carmichael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stokely_Carmichael "Stokely Carmichael"), a leader of the [Black Panther Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Panther_Party "Black Panther Party"), in 1968, and consequently lost support among white Americans. Her visa was revoked by the US government when she was travelling abroad, forcing her and Carmichael to relocate to Guinea. She continued to perform, mostly in African countries, including at several [independence celebrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Africa "Decolonisation of Africa"). She began to write and perform music more explicitly critical of apartheid; the 1977 song "[Soweto Blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto_Blues "Soweto Blues")", written by her former husband [Hugh Masekela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Masekela "Hugh Masekela"), was about the [Soweto uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soweto_uprising "Soweto uprising").
